volumes.title: The Ferry at the Ford
volumes.text:
Emberwick counts its years from a rope. In the year the town calls One, a widow named Maud Fenner stretched a tarred line across the river at the shallow place and began pulling travellers over on a flat raft, a penny a head, sheep at four a penny.

She kept an iron basket of coals burning on the north bank so that carters coming late off the Lowland road could find the crossing in the dark. People said, "Make for the ember." Then, when a dairy and two cottages had gathered round it, they said, "Make for Emberwick," a wick being the old word for a farm that sells its butter. The river took the name as well, in time.

Maud's ferry bell still hangs by the water. It is rung once each New Year, by whoever gets there first.

volumes.title: Seven Households and a Market
volumes.text:
By the Year 12 there were seven households at Emberwick: the Fenners at the ferry, a smith, a dairy, two families of weavers, a cooper, and a man named Hobb who did nothing in particular but was always there.

That autumn the seven agreed, under the oak on the green, to hold a market every Wednesday. No lord granted it. They simply wrote the rules on a board: honest weights, no selling before the bell, and stray pigs to be returned washed. The board hangs in the Guildhall, and the third rule has never been repealed.

The first market offered cheese, nails, one barrel and a quantity of opinions. It took in four shillings. The oak came down in a gale long ago, but Wednesday has gone on being market day ever since, in all weathers.

volumes.title: The First Bridge
volumes.text:
For thirty-seven years everyone who came to Emberwick came by Maud Fenner's ferry, and waited their turn. By the Year 38 the Wednesday market had grown so busy that the queue of carts on the south bank reached back to the Lowland road, and the town decided to build a bridge over the Ember.

It was made of oak, on eleven trestles, by a carpenter named Jory Plank, who was teased about his name every day of the work and answered each time with the same patient nod. Maud Fenner, by then very old, was carried across first in a chair. She said it was quicker but less sociable.

The ferry raft was hauled up the bank and turned over to make the roof of a hen house. Nothing in Emberwick is thrown away if it can keep off rain.

volumes.title: A Mayor by Show of Hats
volumes.text:
Until the Year 52 Emberwick was governed by whoever shouted longest at the Wednesday market. This worked while there were seven households. With ninety it produced sore throats and two different rules about where to tie a horse.

So the townsfolk met on the green to choose one person to do the deciding. There were no ballot papers, paper being dear. Each voter threw a hat toward the candidate preferred, and the hats were counted. Aldous Fenner, grandson of the ferrywoman, received sixty-one hats and one bonnet thrown from a window.

His chain of office was made from the brass rings of the old ferry rope, and every mayor since has worn it. It is heavy and turns the collar green. Mayors are still chosen on the green in June, though hats are now kept on.

volumes.title: The Great Damp
volumes.text:
The Year 66 is remembered in Emberwick as the Great Damp. It rained for thirty days from the first of March, the snow came off the Northern Fells all at once, and the river Ember rose nine feet in a night.

Nobody was lost. The town owes that to old Mayor Fenner, who rowed from door to door in a brewing tub, and to the ferry bell, which was rung until its rope wore through. But the timber bridge went, whole, like a raft. So did the lower street, a great many hen houses, and the smith's anvil, which was later found exactly where it had always been, under two feet of silt.

When the water went down, the town moved itself forty yards up the hill, where it has stood ever since. The old cellars are gardens now, and grow excellent rhubarb.

volumes.title: The Wool Years
volumes.text:
Between the Year 90 and the Year 104, Emberwick grew rich, by its own modest measure, on wool. Fell sheep came down the drove road each June, were shorn on the green, and went home looking embarrassed. The fleeces were washed in the Ember, spun in the cottages, and woven in the long sheds still called Weavers' Row.

Emberwick cloth was a thick grey stuff known as wickset. It was not handsome, but rain ran off it, and Lowland carters would wear nothing else.

With the profits the wool merchants raised the Guildhall in the Year 104, with a carved ram over the door. The ram has lost one horn to weather and one to a boy with a ladder. The trade faded when fashion turned to finer cloth, but the hall remained, and the town has met in it ever since.

volumes.title: The Slow Clock
volumes.text:
In the Year 140 Emberwick built a clock tower on the market square, paid for by a penny on every stall for three years. The clock was made by a travelling clockmaker who left the morning it was finished, which the town later thought significant.

It has always run seven minutes slow. Clockmakers were sent for, weights were shifted, the pendulum was shortened by the width of a thumbnail, and for a week it would keep proper time. Then it would settle back, as a cat returns to its own chair.

Mayor Ezekiel Moss ended the argument by declaring that the clock was right and the sun was early. Emberwick has kept its own time since. Visitors are advised that the Wednesday market opens at eight by the tower, and that the coach will not wait for them.

volumes.title: The Quarrel with Marrowby
volumes.text:
Every town likes to have one war in its history, and Emberwick's lasted from the Year 163 to the Year 171. It was fought against the village of Marrowby, two miles east, over a three-acre goose pasture called Gander Meadow, after the Pennybrook changed its course in a flood and left the meadow on the wrong bank.

The chronicle must record the facts honestly. Eleven geese were impounded. A declaration was sent with a penny too little paid on it. Two small armies met at a stile, were rained upon, and shared a barn. Signposts were turned in the night. Nobody was hurt, though a drum was sat on.

Peace was signed beneath a pear tree, and the meadow has been shared ever since. The fuller account fills twelve volumes of its own, which is a good deal more shelf than three acres deserve.

volumes.title: The Long Frost
volumes.text:
The frost of the Year 190 began in Emberwick on the ninth of December and did not let go until the first week of March. The river Ember froze so hard that a loaded hay cart was driven across beside the bridge, simply to show it could be done.

Mayor Dorcas Bellwether had soup served from the Guildhall every noon and ordered the Wednesday market onto the ice, where it stayed for eleven weeks. There were stalls, skittles, a roasting pit that slowly sank an inch, and a barber who shaved customers in a sledge.

When the thaw came the ice went out in one night with a noise like furniture being moved. It cracked the middle arch of the bridge. A line cut in the Guildhall doorpost shows how deep the snow lay that winter, and children are measured against it still.

volumes.title: Four Thousand Books
volumes.text:
Emberwick Library was founded in the Year 214, somewhat by accident. Mrs Isolde Marram, widow of a sea captain from the Grey Coast, left the town her husband's books: four thousand of them, in forty tea chests, delivered to the Guildhall steps on a wet Tuesday without warning.

Mayor Septimus Vole, who read slowly and admitted it, said that a town given four thousand books had better become the sort of town that deserved them. The council bought the old wool warehouse on Lantern Street, shelved it with oak from the Fells, and hired a librarian at twelve pounds a year and all the candles she needed.

The books arrived in no order at all, and it is said that they have never entirely been put right. Each generation of shelvers has done its best, mostly at night.

volumes.title: The Canal That Stopped
volumes.text:
In the Year 240 a company of gentlemen from the Lowlands proposed to dig a canal to Emberwick, and bring it coal, prosperity and bargemen. Mayor Clementine Rudge was doubtful but polite. Shares were sold. A fine iron footbridge was put up in advance, to carry the meadow path over the water when the water arrived.

The cut reached to within one mile of the town and then met a bed of gravel that drank every drop poured into it. The company dissolved. The bargemen never came.

Emberwick was left with a dry green trench full of primroses, an iron bridge over nothing, and its quiet. Twenty-eight years later Mayor Oake lit the streets with forty lamps instead, which cost less and worked. Most people now agree that the town had a narrow and fortunate escape.

volumes.title: The Three Hundredth Year
volumes.text:
This chronicle closes in the Year 300, three centuries after Maud Fenner stretched her rope across the Ember. The town now has some two thousand people, one bridge of three arches, a clock seven minutes slow, a Wednesday market, a library and a half share in a goose meadow.

On New Year's morning the whole of Emberwick walked down to the water. The youngest Fenner, a girl of six, was lifted up to ring the ferry bell, and an iron basket of coals was lit on the north bank, as on the first night.

I have been Town Chronicler for thirty-one years, and have tried to set down what happened without making it grander than it was. The pen now passes to my successor. There are blank pages left at the back of the book, and I am glad of that.

volumes.title: The Stream Moves
volumes.text:
The Border Wars between the town of Emberwick and the village of Marrowby began with water, in the spring of the Year 163. For as long as anyone had kept records, the boundary between the two parishes had been the Pennybrook, a stream that a child could jump.

That March the brook flooded, and when it settled it was found to be running forty yards east of where it had been. Stranded on its western side lay Gander Meadow: three acres of grass, one pear tree, and the grazing of all Marrowby's geese. The meadow was now, by the plain rule of the brook, in Emberwick.

Emberwick said a boundary was a boundary. Marrowby said a brook was not entitled to give away other people's property. Both were right, which is the worst way for a quarrel to start.

volumes.title: The Affair of the Geese
volumes.text:
In April of the Year 163, a few weeks after the Pennybrook shifted and left Gander Meadow on the Emberwick side, the geese of Marrowby walked across to graze there as they always had. Geese do not read parish maps.

The Emberwick pound-keeper, a careful man named Silas Trott, found eleven of them on what was now town grass and did his duty. He drove them two miles to the pound behind the Guildhall, which took him four hours and cost him the seat of his breeches.

The geese belonged to Mrs Philippa Crake of Marrowby, who arrived the next morning and demanded them back. Trott asked for the usual fine of a penny a head. Mrs Crake said she would sooner eat her hat. The geese stayed, were fed at the town's expense, and grew noticeably stout.

volumes.title: A Declaration by Post
volumes.text:
By May of the Year 163 the dispute over Gander Meadow had reached the council chamber of Emberwick, where Mayor Horatio Pim felt that something official ought to be done. He drafted a Declaration of Stern Displeasure against the village of Marrowby, in three paragraphs, with a seal.

It went by the carrier on a Monday. Unhappily the clerk had paid a penny too little, and the rule was that the receiver made up the difference. Marrowby declined. The village elders said they would not pay a penny to be insulted, and that if Emberwick wanted a war it could afford the postage.

The letter went back to the carrier's office and lay there. For three weeks, strictly speaking, both sides were at peace and did not know it. In the end Mayor Pim walked over and read his copy aloud through Mrs Crake's gate.

volumes.title: The Mustering
volumes.text:
War having been declared in the summer of the Year 163, at least out loud, Emberwick and Marrowby each raised an army to settle the matter of Gander Meadow.

Emberwick's force was the Town Volunteers: fourteen men, one drum, and a pike borrowed from above the Guildhall fireplace, under Captain Barnaby Oddfellow, a candle-maker with a carrying voice. They drilled on the green on Thursdays, since Wednesday was market day and nobody could be spared.

Marrowby mustered nine, but had a brass band of six besides, and gave the command to Mrs Philippa Crake, owner of the impounded geese, with the rank of Colonel. She drilled her troops in the meadow lane on Thursdays too. For some weeks the two armies could hear one another practising across the fields, and each privately thought the other sounded rather good.

volumes.title: The Battle of the Stile
volumes.text:
The only battle of the Border Wars took place on the fourteenth of August in the Year 163, at the stile where the footpath from Emberwick enters Gander Meadow. Fourteen Volunteers under Captain Oddfellow arrived from the west. Nine men of Marrowby and a brass band, under Colonel Crake, arrived from the east.

The stile admits one person at a time. Neither commander would climb it first, since whoever did would be standing alone in front of an army. They discussed this for an hour.

Then it rained, heavily. Both armies ran for Farmer Dunnock's barn, which was the nearest roof, and stayed there until dark. Cards were played. The band obliged with a few tunes. A drum was sat on and never quite recovered. Marrowby won ninepence, and has counted the battle a victory ever since.

volumes.title: The Signpost Campaign
volumes.text:
Through the autumn of the Year 163 the war between Emberwick and Marrowby over Gander Meadow was carried on entirely at night, and entirely by carpentry.

It began when someone from Marrowby pulled up the new Emberwick boundary post and replanted it forty yards west. Emberwick moved it back, and for good measure turned the finger-post at the crossroads so that "Marrowby" pointed into the marsh. Marrowby answered by repainting the Emberwick milestone to read two hundred miles.

Nobody was ever caught, though both blacksmiths did brisk business in nails. The chief sufferer was a travelling pedlar named Fitch, who followed the signs faithfully for a whole day and arrived, at dusk, back where he had started. He sold both places lanterns at a high price, and declared himself satisfied.

volumes.title: The Pear Embargo
volumes.text:
In the second year of the Border Wars, the Year 164, the village of Marrowby tried to win Gander Meadow by trade. It forbade the sale of pears, perry and pear jam to anyone from Emberwick. Marrowby pears were the best in the district, and the blow was felt.

Emberwick replied by refusing to sell Marrowby any candles, the town having the only chandler for ten miles, who was also its Captain of Volunteers. Marrowby went to bed early that winter, and Emberwick ate its cheese plain.

Neither embargo was well kept. Aunts walked between the two places with remarkably heavy baskets. A Marrowby man was seen buying candles disguised in his wife's bonnet, and was served without comment. By spring the trade in secret pears was larger than the open trade had ever been.

volumes.title: The Surveyor's Opinion
volumes.text:
By the Year 165 Emberwick and Marrowby had quarrelled over Gander Meadow for two years, and agreed on one thing only: to hire a surveyor and abide by what he found. They sent to the Lowlands for Mr Ambrose Lint, who came with a brass chain, a boy and a very small dog.

He measured for six days. Then he reported to both councils together, in Farmer Dunnock's barn. The meadow, he said, was three acres and eleven perches. Emberwick's map was wrong. Marrowby's map was also wrong, in a different direction. The oldest deed he could find described the land only as "the goose's".

He charged each side his full fee and left by the morning coach. The two councils walked home separately, having learned what expert advice so often teaches, and the war went on.

volumes.title: The Winter Truce
volumes.text:
The winter of the Year 167 was a hard one, and it interrupted the war between Emberwick and Marrowby in its fifth year. In January the Marrowby mill pond froze to the bottom, the wheel stood still, and the village had grain but no flour.

Captain Oddfellow of the Emberwick Volunteers heard of it on a Monday. On Tuesday twelve sacks of flour went east on a sledge, with a note saying they were a loan between enemies and need not be mentioned. Colonel Crake sent back a crate of pears, the first to cross openly in three years, and a note saying nothing had been received.

Hostilities were then suspended for skating. Both armies used the frozen pond, and the Marrowby band played. The truce lasted until the thaw, and everyone was sorry to see it end.

volumes.title: The Wedding Problem
volumes.text:
In the Year 169, six years into the Border Wars, the drummer of the Emberwick Volunteers asked to marry the daughter of the Marrowby bandmaster. His name was Ned Sallow, hers was Tabitha Horn, and they had met in Farmer Dunnock's barn during the Battle of the Stile, sheltering from the rain.

Nobody objected to the match. The difficulty was the place. Emberwick would not have its drummer married in enemy country, and Marrowby felt the same about its bandmaster's daughter.

Tabitha settled it. She said the one piece of ground that both sides claimed must belong to both, and they were married in Gander Meadow under the pear tree, on a fine June morning. Fourteen Volunteers stood on one side and the band on the other. Eleven very fat geese were let out of the pound for the day.

volumes.title: The Stream Moves Back
volumes.text:
What the Pennybrook began, it also did its best to finish. In the spring of the Year 170, seven years after it first shifted and set Emberwick and Marrowby quarrelling over Gander Meadow, the brook flooded again.

This time it did not choose a side. When the water fell, it was running straight through the middle of the meadow, an acre and a half to the west and an acre and a half to the east, as neatly as if it had been ruled. The pear tree stood on a small island of its own, with water on both sides.

Both councils came to look. They stood on their own banks for some time. Then Mayor Pim of Emberwick remarked that he supposed that was that, and Colonel Crake said she had been thinking much the same.

volumes.title: The Treaty of the Pear Tree
volumes.text:
The Border Wars ended on Midsummer Day in the Year 171, when Emberwick and Marrowby signed the Treaty of the Pear Tree on a table carried over the water into Gander Meadow for the purpose. It has three clauses. The meadow belongs to both parishes. Geese of either may graze it. Nobody is to mention the signposts.

The eleven impounded geese were returned to Mrs Crake after eight years, with their descendants, numbering fifty-four. She waived the question of the fine, and Emberwick waived the bill for feed.

Each Midsummer since, the two places have held a tug of war across the Pennybrook, and the losers are pulled in. The original Declaration of Stern Displeasure is still at the carrier's office in Emberwick, unopened, with a penny owing on it. No one has offered to pay.

volumes.title: Aldous Fenner, the First
volumes.text:
Aldous Fenner became the first Mayor of Emberwick in the Year 52, chosen by a show of hats on the green. He was grandson to Maud Fenner, who founded the ferry, and had inherited her broad shoulders and her habit of counting everything twice.

He was mayor for fourteen years and made three laws: carts keep to the left on the bridge, the market bell is rung at eight, and nobody empties a bucket from an upper window without calling out first. All three stand.

His great hour came at the end. In the flood of the Year 66 he went from door to door in a brewer's tub, at the age of seventy, lifting neighbours from their windows. He retired the following week, saying he had done enough rowing for one family, and kept bees until he died.

volumes.title: Gwendolen Ashby Moves the Town
volumes.text:
Gwendolen Ashby was elected the second Mayor of Emberwick in the Year 66, a week after the great flood, while the lower street was still under silt. She was a builder's widow who ran the yard herself, and she is said to have accepted the chain with a trowel in her other hand.

Her decision was simple and unpopular: the town would move forty yards up the hill. She paced out the new market square herself and marked the corners with four of her own bricks, which are there yet. Those who complained were lent a shovel.

In fourteen years she saw every household rehoused above the flood line and a new bridge raised in stone. She never made a speech longer than a minute. Asked for her secret, she said that mortar sets whether or not you talk to it.

volumes.title: Osric Tulley, the Sleeping Mayor
volumes.text:
Osric Tulley was Mayor of Emberwick from the Year 80 to the Year 101, the third to wear the chain, and for most of that time he was asleep. He was a miller, stout and amiable, and the warmth of the council chamber overcame him within minutes of every meeting.

The council learned to manage. Motions were read out, a pause was left, and if the mayor did not object he was held to have agreed. In twenty-one years he objected once, to a draught.

Historians have been unkind to him, but the facts are awkward for them. Under Tulley the wool trade arrived, the population doubled and the rates were never raised. It may be that a town sometimes needs a mayor who will leave it alone. His portrait in the Guildhall shows him with his eyes shut.

volumes.title: Marigold Thrupp and the Guildhall
volumes.text:
Marigold Thrupp, fourth Mayor of Emberwick, served from the Year 101 to the Year 109. She was a wool merchant who had begun with one borrowed ewe, and she could tell the weight of a fleece by lifting a corner of it.

Her monument is the Guildhall, finished in the Year 104 and paid for entirely by the wool merchants, herself the first and largest giver. She checked the mason's accounts every Friday and found, over three years, a total error of fourpence, in the town's favour, which she returned.

She disliked waste to a remarkable degree. The Guildhall has one window fewer on the north side than on the south because, she said, nobody needs to look at the north. On leaving office she handed over a surplus of four pounds, a spare roof slate and a list of who still owed what.

volumes.title: Bartholomew Crane, Lover of Ceremony
volumes.text:
Bartholomew Crane was the fifth Mayor of Emberwick and held office from the Year 109 to the Year 131. He was a tailor, and he believed that a town was not properly a town until it had processions.

In twenty-two years he gave Emberwick nearly all its customs. He invented the Beating of the Bounds, in which the council walks the parish edge each May and taps the boundary stones with willow wands. He designed the mayor's three-cornered hat, the beadle's blue coat, and a march for two fifes that nobody has managed to forget.

He also proposed a town motto in an ancient tongue, but since no one could agree on what it meant, it was quietly dropped. Crane retired at eighty with a procession of his own devising. It took four hours to pass the Guildhall and was much enjoyed, chiefly by him.

volumes.title: Ezekiel Moss and the Clock
volumes.text:
Ezekiel Moss, sixth Mayor of Emberwick, served from the Year 131 to the Year 148 and is remembered for one sentence. He was a corn dealer, a calm man with large hands, who disliked arguments because they made people late.

In the Year 140 the town built its clock tower, and the clock at once began to run seven minutes slow. For two years the council debated it. Clockmakers came and went. The baker opened by the sun and the school by the tower, and children arrived at lessons having already eaten their dinners.

Moss rose at last and said, "The clock is right, and the sun is early." It was put to the vote and carried. He governed peacefully for six years more, and was never once late for anything, by the only clock that mattered.

volumes.title: Lettice Underbough, Planter of Limes
volumes.text:
Lettice Underbough was the seventh Mayor of Emberwick, from the Year 148 to the Year 160. She kept a seed shop on Lantern Street and was known to judge people by the state of their window boxes.

Her twelve years were the quietest in the town's record. What she did was plant: forty lime trees along the road to the bridge, a row of pears behind the Guildhall, and a horse chestnut on the green to replace the old market oak, which had blown down before her grandmother was born.

She was mocked for it at the time, trees being slow and the rates not. But she planted every one herself, with a spade that now hangs in the council chamber. The limes meet overhead today. In July the whole avenue hums with bees and smells of honey as far as the water.

volumes.title: Horatio Pim, the War Mayor
volumes.text:
Horatio Pim, eighth Mayor of Emberwick, served from the Year 160 to the Year 172, and so had the misfortune to be in office for the whole of the Border Wars with Marrowby. He was a stationer by trade and loved a well-drafted document above most things.

It was Pim who wrote the Declaration of Stern Displeasure in the Year 163, and Pim whose clerk paid a penny too little to send it. It is said he could never afterwards pass the carrier's office without crossing the street.

Yet he also wrote the Treaty of the Pear Tree, in the Year 171, and it is a model of its kind: three clauses, no long words, and room at the bottom for everyone to sign. He retired the next year and took up fishing in the Pennybrook, from whichever bank he pleased.

volumes.title: Dorcas Bellwether in the Frost
volumes.text:
Dorcas Bellwether was the ninth Mayor of Emberwick, from the Year 172 to the Year 195. She kept the Ferry Bell inn, and had the innkeeper's gift of knowing at a glance who was cold, who was hungry and who was about to cause trouble.

She was sixty-eight when the Long Frost came in the Year 190, and it was the making of her name. For eleven weeks she had soup served from the Guildhall at noon, begged coal from every cellar that had it, and sent the Volunteers to knock each morning on the doors of the old. When the river froze solid she moved the market onto it, saying people needed something to look at.

Not one household went without a fire that winter. She served five years more, and when she stepped down the town gave her a silver ladle. She used it.

volumes.title: Septimus Vole and the Library
volumes.text:
Septimus Vole, tenth Mayor of Emberwick, held office from the Year 195 to the Year 223. He was a carter's son who had left school at nine, and he read with one finger under the line, moving his lips, all his life.

In the Year 214 forty tea chests of books arrived on the Guildhall steps, the bequest of a sea captain's widow. Half the council wished to sell them. Vole would not hear of it. He said he had wanted books as a boy the way other boys wanted apples, and that no child in Emberwick should want them so again.

He found the warehouse on Lantern Street, bargained for the oak, and carried the first chest in himself. In his last years he was seen in the reading room most evenings, working slowly through a history of bridges, one finger under the line.

volumes.title: Clementine Rudge, Thirty-Six Years
volumes.text:
Clementine Rudge was the eleventh Mayor of Emberwick and the longest in office, from the Year 223 to the Year 259. She was the schoolmistress, and for thirty-six years she governed the council much as she had governed the lower form, with patience and a small brass bell.

Her hardest test was the canal scheme of the Year 240. Gentlemen from the Lowlands promised barges and fortunes. Rudge did the sums on a slate, found that they did not come out, and said so; but the town was eager, and she let it learn by doing. When the cut ran dry a mile short, she did not say she had told them. She merely had primroses planted along it.

By the end she had taught half the council their letters. She retired at eighty, and they stood up when she left the room.

volumes.title: Wilfred Oake and the Lamps
volumes.text:
Wilfred Oake, twelfth Mayor of Emberwick, served from the Year 259 to the Year 288. He was an ironmonger, a shy, exact man who walked the streets after dark because, he said, a mayor should know what his town is like when nobody is showing it to him.

What it was like was dark. In the Year 268 he had forty lamps set up, from the bridge to the library door, and hired two lamplighters. He lit the first himself, on the third attempt, in a wind. Old people complained that they could no longer see the stars from the market square, and Oake had the three lamps there fitted with shutters.

Here these Lives end. There have been mayors since, but they are living, and may borrow this book. It is kinder, and safer, to let them wait their turn.

volumes.title: Before There Were Bridges
volumes.text:
The history of bridges at Emberwick must begin with their absence. Before the town had a name, the river Ember was crossed at a shallow place where the bed is gravel and the water, in a dry summer, comes to a tall man's knee. Drovers waded it. Sheep were persuaded.

In the year the town calls One, Maud Fenner improved on wading with a rope ferry: a flat raft hauled hand over hand along a tarred line. It carried six people, or one cart, or twenty sheep if they were tired.

A ferry is a kind of bridge that moves, and has the same purpose, which is to save people from getting wet. For thirty-seven years it was all Emberwick had. On a low day in August you can still see the gravel of the ford from the present bridge, pale under the water.

volumes.title: Maud's Bridge
volumes.text:
The first true bridge at Emberwick was built in the Year 38 and named for the ferrywoman, Maud Fenner, who had carried the town across the Ember for a generation. It was the work of a carpenter named Jory Plank and took one summer.

It stood on eleven oak trestles driven into the gravel of the ford, with a deck of split logs laid crossways and a handrail on the upstream side only, timber being short. It was nine feet wide. Two carts could not pass, and the rule was that the one going downhill gave way.

It creaked. People called this "Maud talking". On frosty mornings the deck was strewn with ashes from the ferry coals, a duty that fell to the youngest Fenner. The bridge served twenty-eight years, which for unpainted oak in running water is an honourable life.

volumes.title: The Bridge That Left
volumes.text:
In the flood of the Year 66, known in Emberwick as the Great Damp, the river Ember rose nine feet in a night and Maud's Bridge, the town's first, went away. It did not break. The eleven trestles lifted out of the gravel together and the whole thing floated off downstream, deck uppermost, like a very long raft.

Witnesses said a cat was sitting on it. This cannot now be proved.

The bridge was found three days later, two miles down, lying across a pasture as if it had meant to cross something there. The farmer claimed it by right of arrival and made the deck into a barn floor. Bridge Barn still stands, and the log planks are worn pale by two centuries of boots. The town was left with a ford, a rowing boat and a strong wish to build in stone.

volumes.title: Three Arches of Stone
volumes.text:
The stone bridge at Emberwick was begun in the Year 67 and opened in the Year 71, under Mayor Gwendolen Ashby, after the flood that carried off its timber forerunner. It has three arches and is the same bridge the town uses now.

The mason was Hulda Garth, brought down from the Northern Fells with her own quarrymen. She pointed their upstream ends like the bows of boats to part the floodwater, and made the middle arch the widest, at thirty feet. The stone is a grey grit that goes almost silver in rain.

She was asked how long it would last. She said she had built it for the worst night she could imagine, and then a little more. On the keystone, downstream side, she cut a small ferry bell. You have to lean over to see it.

volumes.title: The Egg Toll
volumes.text:
From its opening in the Year 71 the stone bridge at Emberwick charged a toll, to pay back what the building had cost. A toll house the size of a cupboard stood at the town end, and in it sat a keeper with a ledger.

The charge was a halfpenny for a person, a penny for a cart, and nothing for anyone carrying a baby. Coin was scarce in the district, so the rule allowed payment in kind: one egg was taken as a halfpenny. On market days the keeper might take two hundred eggs before noon.

The ledgers survive. They record forty-nine years of eggs, a few buttons, and one entry reading "a song, badly". The debt was cleared in the Year 120 and the toll was ended. The last keeper, it is written, never willingly ate an omelette again.

volumes.title: The Packhorse Bridge
volumes.text:
During the wool years, Emberwick cloth went east to market on the backs of ponies, and in the Year 98 the wool merchants paid for a bridge over the Pennybrook on the Marrowby road, so that the pack trains need not ford it.

It is a single steep arch, humped like a cat, and only five feet wide. The parapets are no higher than a man's knee. That was deliberate: a loaded pony is widest at the pack, and low walls let the bales swing clear on either side. Twenty ponies crossed nose to tail, with a bell on the leader.

The wool trade is gone, and carts take the newer road. But the packhorse bridge is still there under its ivy, and is still the quickest way to Marrowby on foot. Walkers should know that there is nothing whatever to hold on to.

volumes.title: The Clapper in the Fells
volumes.text:
The oldest bridge in the district is not at Emberwick at all. It lies a long day's walk north, where the drove road crosses the young river Ember in the Northern Fells: five great slabs of stone laid flat on four piles of boulders. Such a bridge is called a clapper.

Nobody knows who built it. The shepherds say a giant set it down so as not to wet her stockings, which is as good an account as any. It enters the written record only in the Year 133, when a spate tipped the middle slab into the river and Emberwick sent twelve men and two oxen to put it back.

It took them nine days. The slab is said to weigh four tons. They left their initials underneath, where only trout can read them, and went home with a new respect for the giant.

volumes.title: The Marsh Causeway
volumes.text:
West of Emberwick, downstream, the land sinks into marsh, and for most of the town's history the only way across was to go round. In the Year 155 the council resolved to build a bridge over ground too soft to hold one.

The answer was a causeway that floats. Bundles of hazel and alder, each as thick as a barrel, were laid crossways on the peat in a line a mile long, with oak planks pegged over all. It gives underfoot like a mattress. Herons use the handrail.

It also sinks, about an inch a year, and has done from the start. The remedy is to lay new bundles on the old, so that the causeway of today rests on seven or eight earlier ones, going down into the dark. It is, in its way, the deepest bridge in the district.

volumes.title: The Bridge of Two Halves
volumes.text:
When Emberwick and Marrowby made peace in the Year 171, after eight years of quarrelling over Gander Meadow, they agreed to build a footbridge across the Pennybrook beside the pear tree, as a sign of friendship. Each parish would build half. They would meet in the middle.

Each parish also, it turned out, used its own carpenter, its own measuring rod and its own idea of level. On the day the halves were joined, the Marrowby side was found to be eleven inches higher than the Emberwick side.

There was a silence. Then old Captain Oddfellow observed that a step was not the same as a gap, and a single oak tread was fitted between. It is there now. Walkers cross from one parish to the other by going up or down one stair, and most do not know why.

volumes.title: Ice Against the Arches
volumes.text:
The hardest test of Emberwick's stone bridge came in the Year 190, at the end of the Long Frost, when it was a hundred and nineteen years old. The river Ember had been frozen for eleven weeks. Then, in one night of warm rain, the ice broke.

It came down in slabs the size of barn doors and piled against the piers as high as the parapet. The bridgewarden watched from the bank with a lantern and could do nothing. Near dawn there was a sound like a gate slamming, and a crack ran up through the middle arch.

The arch held. In summer it was stitched with nine iron cramps, set in lead, which can be counted from a boat. Hulda Garth, its mason, had built for the worst night she could imagine and a little more. This was the little more.

volumes.title: The Dry Bridge
volumes.text:
The strangest bridge near Emberwick crosses no water at all. It was put up in the Year 241, during the canal scheme, to carry the meadow footpath over a canal that was confidently expected within the year.

It is made of cast iron, in a single shallow arch of forty feet, with a railing of iron bulrushes and the company's initials at the centre. It arrived in pieces on six wagons and was bolted together in a week. It was, everyone agreed, the handsomest thing the canal produced.

The canal itself stopped a mile short of the town, when the cut would not hold water. So the Dry Bridge spans a grassy trench full of primroses, and has done for nearly sixty years. Children roll down the banks beneath it. It is painted green every seventh spring, and has never had the smallest trouble with damp.

volumes.title: All the Bridges in a Day
volumes.text:
To close this history, in the summer of the Year 300, I walked to every bridge in it that one day allows. I am Bridgewarden of Emberwick, as my mother was, and thought it time I inspected the whole inheritance.

I started on the Dry Bridge at dawn, went springily over the marsh causeway, and looked in at Bridge Barn, where the floor is still Maud's deck. Then I turned east, crossed the packhorse bridge holding on to nothing, and took the one step up at Gander Meadow. The clapper in the Fells was too far, and must take my word.

At sunset I stood on the middle arch of the stone bridge. The ford showed pale below. I leaned over to see Hulda Garth's little bell on the keystone, and nearly lost my hat. Everything was sound. All of it is still carrying people over, dry.
